title: Bathtub Grab Bars and Safety Rails: How to Choose the Right One
subtitle: A plain-English guide to clamp-on tub rails, wall-mounted grab bars and bath seats, and what each one can and cannot do.
excerpt: Stepping in and out of the tub is one of the trickiest moves in the house. Here is how clamp-on rails, wall grab bars and bath seats compare, and what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Getting into and out of a bathtub asks a lot of the body. You lift one leg over a high wall, balance on a wet, slippery surface, and then do it all again on the way out. For many people, that is the moment when a little extra support matters most.
A handhold or a seat can help, but the right kind depends on your tub, your walls and the person who will be using it. This guide walks through the choices and what to check before you buy.
Bathroom safety products tend to fall into three groups. Each solves a slightly different problem.

These rails attach to the side wall of the bathtub itself. They give you something to hold while you step over the tub wall. They only fit some tubs, so check the wall thickness and the tub material against the listing. A clamp-on rail is a steadying handhold, not a replacement for a bar fastened into the wall studs or a proper anchor.

These are fastened into the wall, into the studs behind it or with a proper anchor (a special fastener made to hold weight). Consumer Reports suggests looking for bars that are ADA-compliant (meaning they meet Americans with Disabilities Act guidelines) or that meet the accessibility standard known as A117.1. It also suggests installing bars horizontally, 33 to 36 inches high, beside the toilet and in the shower or tub.
Consumer Reports notes that a shower bench can give support or a place to rest. A seat needs enough space in the tub or stall, so check the seat height and the width of your tub before you order.
"Don't place towel bars where you might be tempted to grab them; they aren't designed to support you." (Consumer Reports, "How to Create a Safer, More Comfortable Bathroom")

items: Weight capacity: Check the stated number. If a listing does not give one, ask the maker or seller before you buy.
Fit: For clamp-on rails, check your tub wall's thickness and material against the listing. For bath seats, check the seat height and the width of your tub or stall.
Standards: For wall bars, Consumer Reports suggests looking for ADA-compliant bars or ones that meet A117.1.
Installation cost: Professional installation of wall bars is a hidden cost, and so is shipping for chairs. Factor both into your budget.
Returns: Check the return window in case the product does not fit your tub or wall.
Who it is for: If someone cannot step over the tub wall or needs hands-on help, talk with a doctor or occupational therapist about options such as a transfer bench.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well
For a clamp-on rail, follow the maker's instructions and double-check the fit against your tub wall before you rely on it.

For a wall-mounted bar, think about how you actually move. Where do you reach as you step in? Where do you want to hold as you stand up from a seat? Consumer Reports suggests horizontal bars 33 to 36 inches high beside the toilet and in the shower or tub, so keep that in mind when you plan.
If you add a bath seat, measure your tub first so the seat fits with room to spare. The AquaSense listing says its legs have non-skid tips and its seat height adjusts.

A clamp-on tub rail helps you steady yourself as you step over the tub wall. It does not replace a wall grab bar fastened into studs or a proper anchor, and no rail or bar can prevent every fall. Towel bars are not designed to hold your weight, so do not use them for support.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A good handhold can make bath time calmer and steadier. Measure your tub, check the weight limit, and ask your doctor or an occupational therapist if you are unsure what suits you. A little planning now can make every bath feel more secure.

products.name: Drive Medical 22 in. x 1 in. Bathtub Grab Bar Safety Rail, White (rtl12036-adj)
products.blurb: A tub rail for people who want a handhold when stepping over the tub wall, designed to fit most bathtub styles. Height adjusts from 14 to 17 inches and rubber pads protect the tub; the listing does not state a weight capacity, so confirm it with the seller. 90-day returns, in store or online.

products.name: Moen Home Care 18-in Glacier grab bar (R8718W)
products.blurb: A wall-mount, ADA-compliant bar for anyone who wants a bar fastened into the wall, with a 500-lb weight capacity. Also sold in a 24-inch length; installation cost may be extra, since professional installation of wall bars is a common hidden cost.

products.name: Drive Medical AquaSense Adjustable Bath Seat with Backrest
products.blurb: Suits people who would rather sit while bathing, with a rust-resistant aluminum frame that supports up to 300 lbs. The seat height adjusts and the legs have non-skid tips; it needs enough space in your tub, so measure first.
